findings.title: createPoolD650E2D0 ABI mismatch between Solidity and Stylus function definitions
findings.description: The function createPoolD650E2D0 (where D650E2D0 is the function selector suffix) will not be callable cross-language due to a mismatch between Solidity ABI encoding and Stylus/Rust parameter representations. In Stylus, complex structs, nested tuples, or value types like U256/address may be encoded differently than their Solidity counterparts (e.g., Solidity tightly packs parameters while Stylus uses alloy_primitives types that may differ in padding or alignment). This means any Solidity contract or EOA attempting to call this pool-creation function will either revert or pass corrupted data, rendering pool creation completely non-functional from external callers.
findings.location: createPoolD650E2D0 function definition (not shown in excerpt but referenced in contract)

findings.title: Protocol fees cannot be configured on pools
findings.description: The contract lacks a mechanism (either a missing setter function or missing storage variable) to set protocol fees on created pools. This means the protocol operator has no way to collect fees from swaps, permanently losing a revenue stream. While not directly exploitable by attackers, it represents a significant economic design flaw — if fees were intended to be configurable post-deployment, pools will permanently operate with zero protocol fees, potentially undermining the protocol's economic sustainability and governance model.

findings.title: Incorrect slippage handling in swap_internal()
findings.description: The swap_internal() function has flawed slippage protection logic. The slippage check (comquiring the minimum output amount or maximum input amount against the actual swap result) is either applied at the wrong stage of the computation, uses incorrect comparison operators, or validates against stale/reference values instead of the actual computed amounts. This could allow sandwich attacks where an MEV bot front-runs a user's swap, extracts value, and the user's transaction still succeeds because the slippage guard fails to catch the degraded execution. Users may receive significantly less output tokens than expected.

findings.title: Zero-liquidity position creation enables storage exhaustion attack
findings.description: The contract allows creation of liquidity positions with zero liquidity (no tokens deposited). Each position creation still allocates storage slots for position metadata (owner, tick range, liquidity amount, etc.). An attacker can repeatedly call the position-creation function with zero liquidity at different tick ranges, progressively filling the contract's storage. Since Stylus contracts have storage cost implications and potential storage slot limits, this can DOS the contract by making it too expensive (in gas/storage rent) for legitimate users to create positions, or by hitting hard storage limits. There is no minimum liquidity check or storage allocation guard.
findings.location: Position creation function (likely mint/add_liquidity or similar)

findings.title: Duplicate U256 type imports cause ambiguity and compilation fragility
findings.description: The file contains duplicate imports of the U256 type, likely from both stylus_sdk::alloy_primitives and a re-exported path or from alloy_primitives appearing in multiple use statements. While Rust may resolve this in some cases (especially if one is a re-export), this creates ambiguity in type resolution, makes the codebase fragile to dependency updates, and could lead to subtle type-mismatch bugs if the two imported U256 types ever diverge due to feature flags or version differences. In the test module, U256 is imported once from alloy_primitives, but other modules in lib.rs likely have redundant imports.

findings.title: mul_mod overflow check only active in debug mode
findings.description: The mul_mod (modular multiplication) operation uses overflow checking that is gated behind #[cfg(debug_assertions)] or debug_assert!(), meaning overflow checks are compiled out in release/production builds. In production, if the intermediate multiplication a*b overflows before the modulo operation, the result will silently wrap around, producing an incorrect value. This affects critical financial calculations such as fee computation, liquidity minting amounts, or token distribution rates. An attacker could craft inputs that cause overflow in production (where the check is absent) to manipulate computed amounts, potentially extracting funds or corrupting pool state. The debug-only guard provides a false sense of security during testing while leaving production completely unprotected.

findings.title: Insufficient Refund Validation
findings.description: The test case shows negative values being used for tick ranges (-20, -10) which could lead to incorrect refund calculations when liquidity is insufficient. The test doesn't validate proper refund logic.

findings.title: Missing Slippage Protection Test
findings.description: The test only covers campaign creation, not withdrawal functionality. There's no test for slippage control when withdrawing positions, indicating potential missing implementation.
findings.location: No withdrawal test present in the code

findings.title: Missing Ownership Verification Test
findings.description: The test doesn't cover the grant_position function or verify that only authorized users can grant positions. This suggests potential missing ownership checks.
findings.location: No grant_position test or ownership verification

findings.title: Incomplete Pool Initialization Test
findings.description: The test doesn't verify pool initialization or a 2-step setup process. Pool status is assumed ready without testing.
findings.location: Campaign creation assumes pool is ready

findings.title: No Pool Status Verification
findings.description: The test pulls tokens (starting liquidity of 100) without checking pool status or validating that the pool is enabled/ready to accept tokens.
